purpose: This tool lets you test whether a game is worth playing. You build the expected value from chances times prizes, then run the game many times and watch the average settle near it.

stops.title: The picture
stops.text: The picture changes with each activity. In the first one you see a spinner with coloured sectors, a table of prize, chance and chance times prize, and below it a graph of your average net per spin. Nothing on the picture is draggable.
stops.try: Answer question 1 in the panel. A table row fills in.

stops.title: Eight activities
stops.text: 1 builds an expected value. 2a to 2c compare options and place them on a number line. 3 uses data from free throws. 4a to 4c let you set a prize, price or ticket count with a slider to reach a goal.
stops.try: Pick 4a and move the prize slider until the game is fair.

stops.title: What Next does
stops.text: Each step jumps to the start of a group: build it, decide between games, use data, then set a number to reach a goal. The questions in the panel are the same for steps and menu.

stops.title: Play the game
stops.text: Play 1 spins once. The bigger buttons spin many times at once. The average net so far moves toward the expected net. A few spins swing a lot. Reset clears the plays.
stops.try: Press Play 1 five times, then Play 1,000. Compare the averages.

stops.title: Quick check
stops.text: A short exit ticket. Each answer is explained.

teacher: Have students predict whether the game is fair before building the bars, then use Play 1,000 to show the average approaching the expected net. Ask: does a negative expected net mean you lose every time? Misconception: expecting the average of a few plays to match exactly.
